meta.name: Drug classes
meta.about: Drug classes: how a family of medicines works, what it targets in the body, which conditions it treats and which medications on this site belong to it. Educational, not prescribing advice.

calcium-channel-blockers.name: Calcium channel blockers
calcium-channel-blockers.summary: Medicines that relax the muscle in artery walls (and, for some members, slow the heart) by blocking the calcium channels those muscles need to contract. Used mainly for high blood pressure and angina.
calcium-channel-blockers.mechanism: Muscle cells contract when calcium enters through L-type channels in their membrane. Blocking the channel leaves arterial smooth muscle relaxed, so arteries widen, resistance falls and blood pressure drops; coronary arteries widen too, improving supply in angina. The dihydropyridines (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine) act almost only on vessels. Verapamil and diltiazem also block the channels in the heart's conduction tissue and muscle, slowing the rate and reducing force, which makes them useful for fast rhythms but hazardous with beta blockers or in heart failure.
calcium-channel-blockers.target: L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac conducting tissue
classEffects: Ankle swelling, flushing and headache from vessel widening (dihydropyridines)
Slow heart rate, constipation and heart block risk (verapamil, diltiazem)
Gum overgrowth with long use
cautions: Verapamil and diltiazem should not be combined with beta blockers or used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Grapefruit juice raises levels of several members
Severe aortic stenosis and unstable angina need specialist advice

classWarnings.text: Dihydropyridines cause dose-related ankle swelling, flushing and headache from vasodilation; verapamil and diltiazem slow the heart and can cause heart block and heart failure, and are not combined with beta blockers.
Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, significant aortic stenosis and, for the dihydropyridines, unstable angina.

classInteractions.effect: Amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil raise simvastatin levels and the risk of myopathy; the simvastatin dose is limited (20 mg with amlodipine).

classInteractions.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, some HIV medicines) and grapefruit
classInteractions.effect: Raise calcium channel blocker levels, increasing hypotension and oedema.
Additive slowing of the heart and negative inotropy: bradycardia, heart block, heart failure; the combination is avoided.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

ace-inhibitors.name: ACE inhibitors
ace-inhibitors.summary: Medicines ending in -pril that block the enzyme which makes angiotensin II, lowering blood pressure, unloading a failing heart and protecting the kidneys in diabetes.
ace-inhibitors.mechanism: The kidneys release renin when pressure or salt falls; renin makes angiotensin I, and angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lungs and vessels turns it into angiotensin II, which constricts arteries, releases aldosterone (salt and water retention) and thickens heart muscle. Blocking the enzyme removes all of these effects, and the pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, which slows the leak of protein in diabetic kidney disease. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so it accumulates and causes the characteristic dry cough.
ace-inhibitors.target: Angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lung and vessel endothelium
classEffects: Dry cough in 10-15%
First-dose dizziness
Raised potassium and a small rise in creatinine
cautions: Never in pregnancy
Angio-oedema (swelling of lips, tongue, throat) means stop for good and avoid the whole class
Pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration to protect the kidneys
Avoid with potassium supplements and most NSAIDs

classWarnings.text: Kidney function and potassium must be checked before starting, 1-2 weeks after starting and after each dose change; angioedema is a rare class effect that can occur at any time.
Contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal toxicity) and after angioedema with an ACE inhibitor; not combined with an ARB or, in diabetes, with aliskiren.

classInteractions.effect: Reduced blood-pressure effect and increased risk of acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, especially with a diuretic as well (the 'triple whammy').

classInteractions.with: Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes
classInteractions.effect: Hyperkalaemia.
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade: more hypotension, kidney injury and hyperkalaemia without extra benefit; not recommended.

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

classInteractions.effect: Reduced lithium excretion and toxicity; levels are monitored.
Contraindicated: greatly increased angioedema risk; a 36-hour washout is required.

duplicationRule.text: Two ACE inhibitors together, or an ACE inhibitor with an ARB, duplicate renin-angiotensin blockade and increase the risk of kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and hypotension without extra benefit.

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

angiotensin-receptor-blockers.name: Angiotensin receptor blockers
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -sartan that block the receptor angiotensin II acts on. They do the same job as ACE inhibitors without the cough, and are the usual alternative when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.mechanism: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by binding AT1 receptors on arterial muscle, the adrenal cortex and heart muscle. ARBs occupy those receptors so the hormone cannot act: arteries relax, aldosterone falls and the heart and kidneys are spared its growth-promoting effects. Because ACE is untouched, bradykinin is not raised and cough and angio-oedema are rare.
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.target: AT1 angiotensin II receptors in vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex and myocardium
classEffects: Dizziness, tiredness
Raised potassium, small rise in creatinine
Rarely angio-oedema
cautions: Never in pregnancy
Not combined with an ACE inhibitor
Sick-day rules as for ACE inhibitors
Monitor kidney function and potassium after starting and after dose changes

classWarnings.text: Kidney function and potassium are monitored as for ACE inhibitors; contraindicated in pregnancy; not combined with an ACE inhibitor or, in diabetes, with aliskiren.

classInteractions.effect: Reduced antihypertensive effect and increased risk of acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.
Hyperkalaemia.
Dual blockade is not recommended (hypotension, kidney injury, hyperkalaemia).

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

classInteractions.effect: Reduced lithium excretion; monitor levels.

duplicationRule.text: An ARB with another ARB or with an ACE inhibitor duplicates renin-angiotensin blockade; UK guidance advises against combining them for hypertension.

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

beta-blockers.name: Beta blockers
beta-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -olol that shield the heart from adrenaline, slowing it and reducing its oxygen demand. Core treatment for angina, after heart attacks, in heart failure and for controlling fast rhythms.
beta-blockers.mechanism: Adrenaline and noradrenaline speed and strengthen the heart through beta-1 receptors. Beta blockers occupy the receptors so the heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, uses less oxygen and lets fewer atrial impulses through the AV node. Cardioselective members (bisoprolol, metoprolol, atenolol) mostly spare the beta-2 receptors in the airways; non-selective ones (propranolol) block both and can provoke asthma. In heart failure, protecting the heart from chronic adrenaline drive improves survival when started low and increased slowly.
beta-blockers.target: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle and conduction tissue (and beta-2 in airways and vessels for non-selective agents)
classEffects: Tiredness, cold hands and feet, slow pulse
Vivid dreams, erectile dysfunction
Masking of hypoglycaemia warning signs
cautions: Never stop suddenly: rebound angina and fast rhythms
Asthma is a relative contraindication, especially for non-selective agents
Not combined with verapamil or diltiazem
Second- or third-degree heart block

classWarnings.text: Can provoke bronchospasm in asthma (cardioselective agents only with specialist advice); avoid abrupt withdrawal after long use because of rebound angina and arrhythmia; mask the warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia in diabetes.
Contraindicated in asthma with a history of bronchospasm, marked bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock and uncontrolled heart failure.

classInteractions.effect: Additive bradycardia, heart block and heart failure; the combination is avoided.
Beta blockers mask hypoglycaemia and can prolong it.
Additive hypotension and, with clonidine, rebound hypertension on withdrawal.

duplicationRule.text: Two beta blockers together offer no benefit and add bradycardia and hypotension.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

statins.name: Statins
statins.summary: The main cholesterol-lowering medicines. They cut LDL cholesterol by 30-55% and reduce heart attacks and strokes in anyone at raised cardiovascular risk.
statins.mechanism: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls how much cholesterol the liver makes. The liver compensates by displaying more LDL receptors, pulling LDL out of the blood. Lower LDL means less cholesterol deposited in artery walls, and statins also stabilise existing plaques so they are less likely to rupture and cause a clot. High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) are used after heart attacks and strokes.
classEffects: Muscle aches in a minority
Headache, digestive upset
Small rise in blood glucose
cautions: Interactions with clarithromycin, some antifungals and ciclosporin; grapefruit with simvastatin
Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine needs a same-day creatine kinase test
Not in pregnancy or active liver disease

references.title: NICE: Cardiovascular disease risk assessment and reduction

classWarnings.text: Muscle toxicity (myopathy, rarely rhabdomyolysis) is the main class hazard; unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine needs a creatine kinase test. Risk rises with dose, interacting drugs, hypothyroidism, kidney impairment and older age.
Contraindicated in active liver disease and in pregnancy and breastfeeding; liver function is measured before, within 3 months and at 12 months.

source.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

classInteractions.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, ciclosporin, some HIV protease inhibitors) and grapefruit juice
classInteractions.effect: Raise levels of atorvastatin and simvastatin (not rosuvastatin or pravastatin) and the risk of myopathy; doses are limited or the statin paused.
Fatal rhabdomyolysis has occurred; the statin is paused during and for 7 days after systemic fusidic acid.
Additive myopathy risk; gemfibrozil is avoided with statins.
INR may rise when a statin is started or the dose changed; extra INR checks.

duplicationRule.text: Two statins together add muscle and liver toxicity without additional benefit; combinations for extra LDL lowering use ezetimibe or other classes instead.

source.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

loop-diuretics.name: Loop diuretics
loop-diuretics.summary: Powerful diuretics that make the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour. Used to clear fluid in heart failure, kidney and liver disease.
loop-diuretics.mechanism: They block the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that normally reabsorbs a quarter of filtered sodium. Salt that stays in the tubule carries water with it, so urine output rises several-fold. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost as well. Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide) act further along the nephron and are the gentler class used for blood pressure.
loop-diuretics.target: NKCC2 co-transporter in the loop of Henle
classEffects: Frequent urination, thirst, cramps
Low potassium, sodium and magnesium; raised uric acid and glucose
Dizziness from low blood pressure
cautions: Kidney function and electrolytes within a week of starting
Hearing damage with rapid high intravenous doses
Pause on sick days
Interactions with lithium, digoxin, aminoglycosides and NSAIDs

classWarnings.text: Loop diuretics cause dehydration, low potassium, sodium and magnesium, and can precipitate acute kidney injury and gout; electrolytes and kidney function are monitored, and high doses can damage hearing.

classInteractions.effect: Reduced diuretic effect and increased risk of kidney injury.
First-dose hypotension and kidney injury when the person is volume-depleted; the diuretic may be reduced when the ACE inhibitor is started.
Hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity.
Additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

anticoagulants.name: Anticoagulants
anticoagulants.summary: Medicines that slow the clotting cascade to prevent and treat clots in veins and the heart: strokes in atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
anticoagulants.mechanism: Direct oral anticoagulants block a single clotting enzyme: factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran), with a predictable effect that needs no blood-level monitoring. Warfarin instead starves the liver of usable vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX and X are made in inactive form; its effect builds over days and varies with diet and other drugs, so the INR test tunes the dose. Heparins, given by injection, activate antithrombin and are used in hospital and pregnancy.
anticoagulants.target: Factor Xa or thrombin (DOACs); vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver (warfarin)
classEffects: Bruising, nosebleeds, heavier periods
Bleeding from the gut or, rarely, into the brain
cautions: Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless specifically advised
Doses adjusted for kidney function, weight and age
Stopped before surgery on a plan; missed DOAC doses lose protection within a day
Warfarin needs a steady vitamin K intake and INR checks

classWarnings.text: Bleeding is the shared major hazard; signs such as blood in urine or stools, prolonged nosebleeds, coughing or vomiting blood, severe headache or unusual bruising need urgent assessment. Interacting drugs, kidney impairment and older age raise the risk.
Warfarin needs regular INR monitoring and is affected by diet, alcohol, illness and many medicines; DOACs are dosed by kidney function, weight and age and need periodic renal function checks.

classInteractions.effect: Additive bleeding risk, particularly gastrointestinal; avoided unless specifically indicated.
Increased bleeding risk; combinations are used only under specialist direction.

classInteractions.with: Strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers (azole antifungals, some HIV medicines, rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort)
classInteractions.effect: Raise or lower DOAC levels substantially; some combinations are avoided.
Raise the INR by altering vitamin K-producing gut flora or inhibiting metabolism; extra INR checks.

duplicationRule.text: Two anticoagulants together (for example warfarin with a DOAC outside a supervised switch) multiply bleeding risk and are avoided.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

antiplatelets.name: Antiplatelet drugs
antiplatelets.summary: Medicines that stop platelets clumping into the clots that block arteries. The backbone of treatment after heart attacks, strokes and stents.
antiplatelets.mechanism: Platelets plug damaged vessels by sticking to each other; in a diseased artery the plug becomes the clot that causes a heart attack or stroke. Low-dose aspirin permanently disables COX-1 in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane; clopidogrel, ticagrelor and prasugrel block the P2Y12 receptor that responds to ADP. After a stent both are used together for months, because a clot on the stent is a catastrophe.
antiplatelets.target: Platelet COX-1 (aspirin) and P2Y12 ADP receptors (clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel)
classEffects: Bruising and prolonged bleeding
Stomach irritation and ulcers (aspirin)
Breathlessness with ticagrelor
cautions: Not for primary prevention in healthy people
Combined with an anticoagulant only on specialist advice
A proton pump inhibitor protects the stomach in those at risk

classWarnings.text: Bleeding, especially gastrointestinal, is the main class hazard; a proton pump inhibitor is often co-prescribed for those at risk, and antiplatelets are not stopped before procedures without the prescriber's advice, particularly after stents.

classInteractions.effect: Additive bleeding risk; combinations are used only for specific indications under supervision.
Additive gastrointestinal bleeding, and ibuprofen can blunt aspirin's antiplatelet effect if taken beforehand.
Increased gastrointestinal bleeding risk.
Reduce activation of clopidogrel; an alternative PPI is preferred.

duplicationRule.text: Aspirin with another antiplatelet (dual antiplatelet therapy) is a deliberate, time-limited prescription after stents and acute coronary syndromes; taking two antiplatelets without such an indication adds bleeding risk.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

nitrates.name: Nitrates
nitrates.summary: Vasodilators that relieve angina within minutes by relaxing veins and coronary arteries. Available as a spray for attacks and as long-acting tablets for prevention.
nitrates.mechanism: Nitrates release nitric oxide inside vascular smooth muscle, which raises cyclic GMP and relaxes the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and its workload and oxygen demand fall; coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Continuous exposure causes tolerance, so long-acting preparations are timed to leave a nitrate-free interval each day.
nitrates.target: Guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle via nitric oxide
classEffects: Throbbing headache, flushing
Dizziness and fainting from low blood pressure
cautions: Dangerous drop in pressure with sildenafil and similar drugs
Chest pain not relieved by two doses five minutes apart may be a heart attack: call emergency services
Severe aortic stenosis and very low blood pressure

classWarnings.text: Headache, flushing and postural hypotension are common; tolerance develops with continuous exposure, so long-acting nitrates are given with a nitrate-free interval.
Contraindicated with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) because of profound hypotension, and in severe aortic stenosis, hypotension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

classInteractions.effect: Severe, potentially fatal hypotension; contraindicated.
Additive hypotension and fainting.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

nsaids.name: NSAIDs
nsaids.summary: Painkillers that also reduce inflammation and fever: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac and the COX-2 selective coxibs. Excellent for short-term musculoskeletal pain, hazardous when used long term without care.
nsaids.mechanism: NSAIDs block the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, cutting production of prostaglandins, the local messengers that sensitise pain nerves, dilate vessels in inflamed tissue and reset the brain's thermostat in fever. The same prostaglandins protect the stomach lining and keep blood flowing through the kidney, so ulcers, kidney injury, fluid retention and raised blood pressure are the class hazards. COX-2 selective agents spare the stomach somewhat but carry more cardiovascular risk.
classEffects: Indigestion, ulcers and bleeding
Kidney injury, fluid retention, raised blood pressure
Worsening asthma in sensitive people
cautions: Lowest dose for the shortest time, with food
Avoid in kidney disease, heart failure, active ulcers, late pregnancy
Never two NSAIDs together; care with anticoagulants, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate
Topical gels give local relief with far fewer side effects

classWarnings.text: All NSAIDs increase the risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention, raised blood pressure and thrombotic cardiovascular events; the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with gastroprotection where indicated.

Contraindicated with a history of NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, active peptic ulcer, severe heart failure and in the third trimester of pregnancy; avoided in severe kidney or liver impairment and in aspirin-sensitive asthma.

classInteractions.effect: Increased bleeding risk; avoided unless specifically indicated.
Acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, and reduced blood-pressure control.
Increased gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration.
Reduced renal excretion and toxicity of methotrexate and lithium.
Ibuprofen taken before aspirin can block its antiplatelet effect; additive stomach bleeding.

duplicationRule.text: Two NSAIDs together (including aspirin at pain-relief doses, or an oral NSAID with a prescription NSAID such as naproxen) add gastrointestinal, kidney and cardiovascular harm without extra pain relief; UK information advises not taking ibuprofen with similar painkillers without advice.

source.title: NHS: Ibuprofen for adults
source.section: Taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements · Taking ibuprofen with other painkillers

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

non-opioid-analgesics.name: Non-opioid analgesics
non-opioid-analgesics.summary: First-line painkillers without opioid or anti-inflammatory action: paracetamol (acetaminophen) above all, safe at normal doses for most people and most types of mild to moderate pain.
non-opioid-analgesics.mechanism: Paracetamol acts mainly in the central nervous system, weakly inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase in the brain and spinal cord and, through its metabolite AM404, engaging cannabinoid and TRPV1 pathways that raise the pain threshold and lower the fever set-point. It has almost no effect on inflammation or the stomach lining. Its danger is the liver: in overdose a toxic metabolite overwhelms the liver's glutathione and destroys hepatocytes.
non-opioid-analgesics.target: Central cyclo-oxygenase and descending pain pathways
classEffects: Very few at normal doses
Liver failure in overdose
cautions: Maximum 4 g a day for adults, less at low body weight, with alcohol excess or liver disease
Count paracetamol hidden in cold remedies and combination products
Any overdose is an emergency even without symptoms

classWarnings.text: Paracetamol is safe at recommended doses but hepatotoxic in overdose; the maximum daily dose from all products is 4 g for adults, lower at low body weight, in liver disease and in alcohol dependence.

classInteractions.effect: Regular paracetamol can raise the INR; occasional doses do not.

classInteractions.with: Enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin) and chronic alcohol
classInteractions.effect: Increase the toxic metabolite and the risk of liver injury.

duplicationRule.text: Paracetamol is present in many cold remedies and combination painkillers (co-codamol, co-dydramol); taking more than one product containing it risks overdose. UK information advises checking labels and not combining paracetamol products.

source.title: NHS: Paracetamol for adults
source.section: Taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements · Taking paracetamol with other painkillers

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

opioids.name: Opioids
opioids.summary: Strong painkillers that act on the body's own endorphin receptors: morphine, codeine, tramadol, oxycodone, fentanyl. Essential for severe acute pain and cancer pain; harmful when used long term for chronic non-cancer pain.
opioids.mechanism: Opioids bind mu-opioid receptors in the spinal cord, brainstem and brain, closing the gate on pain signals entering the cord and dampening the emotional response to pain. The same receptors in the brainstem slow breathing, in the gut cause constipation, and in the reward pathways produce euphoria and, with repeated use, tolerance and dependence. Naloxone displaces opioids from the receptors and reverses overdose within minutes.
opioids.target: Mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gut
classEffects: Constipation, nausea, drowsiness, itching
Respiratory depression in overdose or with sedatives and alcohol
Tolerance, dependence, addiction
cautions: Start low, review early, plan the stop
Reduce doses in kidney failure and the elderly
Never crush modified-release tablets
No driving while drowsy

classWarnings.text: Respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, dependence and overdose are class hazards; risk rises with other sedatives, alcohol, older age, kidney or liver disease and lung disease. Naloxone reverses overdose.
Long-term use for chronic non-cancer pain has limited evidence of benefit and substantial harm; UK guidance advises against starting opioids for chronic primary pain.

source.title: NICE NG193: Chronic pain (primary and secondary) in over 16s: assessment of all chronic pain and management of chronic primary pain
source.section: 1.2 Managing chronic primary pain: pharmacological management

classInteractions.with: Benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, alcohol and other CNS depressants
classInteractions.effect: Additive sedation and respiratory depression, potentially fatal.
Serotonin syndrome.

classInteractions.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (with fentanyl, oxycodone) and CYP2D6 variation (codeine, tramadol)
classInteractions.effect: Altered opioid levels and effect.

duplicationRule.text: Two opioids together (for example codeine in a combination product with a prescribed strong opioid) add sedation and respiratory depression; combinations are prescribed deliberately, never added over the counter.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

biguanides.name: Biguanides
biguanides.summary: Metformin is the only biguanide in routine use and the first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it lowers glucose without causing hypoglycaemia or weight gain.
biguanides.mechanism: Metformin reduces the glucose the liver pours into the blood by dampening gluconeogenesis, makes muscle and fat more sensitive to insulin so they take up more glucose, and slightly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, which is why it does not cause low blood sugar on its own. HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).
biguanides.target: Hepatic gluconeogenesis (via AMP-activated protein kinase and mitochondrial redox state)
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, bloating at the start
Vitamin B12 deficiency with long use
cautions: Dose reduced below eGFR 45 and stopped below 30
Paused during dehydrating illness and around contrast scans (lactic acidosis risk)
Alcohol in moderation

classWarnings.text: Lactic acidosis is the rare serious hazard: metformin is contraindicated below eGFR 30, paused during dehydrating illness and around iodinated contrast, and avoided in conditions causing hypoxia.
Long-term use lowers vitamin B12; levels are checked when symptoms of deficiency appear and periodically in those at risk.

classInteractions.effect: Risk of contrast-induced kidney injury and metformin accumulation; withheld around the procedure.

classInteractions.with: Drugs that raise blood glucose (corticosteroids, some antipsychotics, thiazides)
classInteractions.effect: Reduced glucose control.

classInteractions.with: Drugs that impair kidney function or compete for renal secretion (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, cimetidine, some antivirals)
classInteractions.effect: Increased metformin levels and lactic acidosis risk.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

insulins.name: Insulins
insulins.summary: Injected replacements for the hormone the pancreas no longer makes or cannot make enough of: essential in type 1 diabetes and used in type 2 diabetes when tablets are not enough.
insulins.mechanism: Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving glucose transporters to the cell surface so glucose leaves the blood, switching the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, and stopping fat breakdown and ketone production. Modern analogues are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro, glulisine) or flat over 24 hours or more as background (glargine, detemir, degludec); mixed and pump regimens mimic the natural pattern of a basal trickle with mealtime bursts.
insulins.target: Insulin receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells
classEffects: Hypoglycaemia
Weight gain
Lumps at injection sites (lipohypertrophy)
cautions: Doses are individual and adjusted for food, activity and illness; 'units' written in full to avoid tenfold errors
Never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, even when not eating
Driving rules: check glucose before and every two hours

classWarnings.text: Hypoglycaemia is the main hazard, more likely with missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney impairment and beta blockers (which mask the warning signs); people on insulin are taught to recognise and treat it and must inform the driving licence authority.

classInteractions.effect: Mask the warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia and can prolong it.
Raise blood glucose; insulin doses may need to increase.

classInteractions.with: ACE inhibitors, alcohol, other glucose-lowering drugs
classInteractions.effect: Increase the risk of hypoglycaemia.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

thyroid-hormones.name: Thyroid hormones
thyroid-hormones.summary: Synthetic thyroxine (levothyroxine) replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring metabolic rate; the dose is tuned by the TSH blood test.
thyroid-hormones.mechanism: Levothyroxine is identical to the thyroid's own T4. Tissues convert it to active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. As levels normalise, the pituitary's TSH falls back into range, which is how the dose is checked. Liothyronine (T3) is used rarely, on specialist advice.
thyroid-hormones.target: Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors in almost every tissue
classEffects: None at the right dose
Palpitations, sweating, weight loss and insomnia if the dose is too high
cautions: Take on an empty stomach, 4 hours apart from calcium, iron, antacids and proton pump inhibitors
Start low in the elderly and in heart disease
Dose often rises in pregnancy: check TSH early
Not for weight loss in people with a normal thyroid

classWarnings.text: Over-replacement causes palpitations, atrial fibrillation, weight loss, anxiety and bone loss; under-replacement leaves hypothyroid symptoms. The dose is adjusted by TSH, rechecked 6-8 weeks after any change.
Started at a low dose in cardiac disease and older people, because a sudden rise in metabolic rate can precipitate angina or arrhythmia.

classInteractions.with: Iron, calcium, antacids, proton pump inhibitors, sucralfate, colestyramine
classInteractions.effect: Reduce levothyroxine absorption; doses are separated by several hours and TSH is monitored.
Increase levothyroxine metabolism; dose may need to rise.
Thyroid status changes warfarin sensitivity; INR monitoring when the dose changes.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

bronchodilators.name: Bronchodilators
bronchodilators.summary: Inhaled medicines that relax the muscle around the airways within minutes (salbutamol, terbutaline) or for 12-24 hours (salmeterol, formoterol, and the antimuscarinics tiotropium and ipratropium). They relieve wheeze but do not treat the inflammation behind asthma.
bronchodilators.mechanism: Beta-2 agonists stimulate beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, raising cyclic AMP so the muscle relaxes and the airway widens. Antimuscarinic bronchodilators block the vagal acetylcholine signal that tightens airways and drives mucus, and are especially useful in COPD. Long-acting beta agonists must be paired with an inhaled steroid in asthma, because used alone they mask worsening inflammation and have been linked to asthma deaths.
bronchodilators.target: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors (agonists) and M3 muscarinic receptors (antimuscarinics) on airway smooth muscle
classEffects: Tremor, fast heartbeat, palpitations, headache (beta agonists)
Dry mouth, urinary retention, glaucoma risk (antimuscarinics)
Low potassium with high doses
cautions: Needing a reliever more than twice a week means the preventer plan needs review
Inhaler technique and spacers matter more than the drug
Beta blockers oppose beta agonists

references.title: NICE: Asthma diagnosis, monitoring and management

classWarnings.text: Increasing reliever use is a sign of worsening asthma and a reason to seek review; high doses cause tremor, palpitations and low potassium. Long-acting beta agonists are used with an inhaled corticosteroid in asthma, never alone.

source.title: NICE NG245: Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management

classInteractions.effect: Antagonise bronchodilation and can provoke bronchospasm.
Additive fall in potassium with high-dose beta agonists.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

corticosteroids.name: Corticosteroids
corticosteroids.summary: Synthetic versions of cortisol that switch off inflammation of any cause: inhaled for asthma, as tablets or injections for flares of many diseases, and as creams, drops and joint injections for local use.
corticosteroids.mechanism: Glucocorticoids enter cells and bind receptors that move to the nucleus, where they switch off genes for inflammatory cytokines and switch on anti-inflammatory ones, shrinking the whole inflammatory response regardless of its trigger. The same receptors in liver, bone, skin, eye and brain produce the side effects of systemic use, and prolonged dosing suppresses the pituitary-adrenal axis, so the body stops making its own cortisol. Inhaled and topical forms deliver tiny doses where they are needed and largely avoid these effects.
corticosteroids.target: Cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors in immune and tissue cells
classEffects: Systemic: raised glucose and blood pressure, weight gain, mood change, thin skin, bone loss, infection risk, cataracts
Inhaled: oral thrush and hoarseness
cautions: Courses over three weeks must be tapered; carry a steroid card
Sick-day and surgery doses; adrenal crisis if stopped abruptly
Bone protection and a proton pump inhibitor for long courses
Live vaccines avoided on high doses

classWarnings.text: Systemic corticosteroids raise blood glucose and blood pressure, thin bone and skin, increase infection risk, disturb mood and sleep, and suppress the adrenal glands; courses over three weeks are tapered, and a steroid card is carried. Chickenpox and measles exposure needs urgent advice in non-immune people.
Inhaled corticosteroids at high doses can also suppress the adrenal glands and affect growth and bone; the lowest dose that controls asthma is used and the mouth is rinsed after use.

classInteractions.effect: Increased gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
Steroids raise glucose; doses of insulin or tablets may need adjusting.
Avoided during high-dose systemic steroid treatment.
Reduce steroid effect; dose may need to rise.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

proton-pump-inhibitors.name: Proton pump inhibitors
proton-pump-inhibitors.summary: The strongest acid-reducing medicines (omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole), which heal ulcers and reflux by shutting down the acid pumps in the stomach lining.
proton-pump-inhibitors.mechanism: PPIs irreversibly block the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the proton pump in parietal cells that secretes acid as the final common step of every stimulus. Acid output falls by over 90% and recovers only as new pumps are made, so the effect outlasts the drug. Taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast when the pumps are most active. H2 blockers (famotidine) are the milder alternative.
proton-pump-inhibitors.target: H+/K+ ATPase in gastric parietal cells
classEffects: Headache, nausea, bowel changes
Low magnesium and B12 with long use
Small increase in gut infections and fractures
cautions: Lowest dose, regular review; rebound acid after stopping
Alarm features (weight loss, swallowing difficulty, bleeding) need endoscopy first
Omeprazole reduces the activation of clopidogrel

classWarnings.text: PPIs can mask gastric cancer; long-term use is associated with low magnesium, fractures, C. difficile infection, vitamin B12 deficiency and subacute cutaneous lupus. The lowest effective dose is used and the need reviewed regularly.

classInteractions.effect: Reduced activation of clopidogrel; lansoprazole or pantoprazole preferred.

classInteractions.with: Drugs whose absorption needs gastric acid (rilpivirine, atazanavir, itraconazole, ketoconazole, some cancer medicines)
classInteractions.effect: Reduced absorption and effect; some combinations contraindicated.
Reduced elimination and toxicity; the PPI may be withheld.
Altered levels or absorption; monitoring advised.

duplicationRule.text: Two PPIs together, or a PPI with an over-the-counter omeprazole product, duplicate acid suppression and its long-term risks.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

penicillins.name: Penicillins
penicillins.summary: The oldest family of antibiotics and still the first choice for many chest, ear, throat, skin and dental infections: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin.
penicillins.mechanism: Penicillins bind the enzymes bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall; growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst. Human cells have no cell wall, which makes the class remarkably selective. Bacteria resist by making beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug; clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav blocks the enzyme, and flucloxacillin is built to withstand the staphylococcal version. They are useless against viruses.
penicillins.target: Penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) in the bacterial cell wall
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, thrush
Rash; anaphylaxis in true allergy (rare)
Clostridioides difficile colitis with broad-spectrum use
cautions: Most reported penicillin allergies are not true allergy and can be assessed; true anaphylaxis excludes the whole class
Amoxicillin causes a rash in glandular fever
Every unnecessary course drives resistance

classWarnings.text: Anaphylaxis in true penicillin allergy is the class hazard; a previous immediate reaction to any penicillin is a contraindication to all of them. Most people labelled penicillin-allergic are not, and formal delabelling widens their antibiotic options.
Antibiotic-associated colitis (C. difficile) can follow any course; severe or persistent diarrhoea needs assessment.

classInteractions.effect: INR may rise; extra checks during and after the course.
Reduced excretion of methotrexate and increased toxicity.
Inactivated by antibacterials; avoided for 3 days before and after.
Increased incidence of rash.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

antihistamines.name: Antihistamines
antihistamines.summary: Medicines that block histamine's H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and itching. Newer members (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) cause little drowsiness; older ones (chlorphenamine, promethazine) sedate.
antihistamines.mechanism: When mast cells release histamine in an allergic reaction, it makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways. Antihistamines occupy the H1 receptors so these effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, which is why they are much less sedating. They are adjuncts only in anaphylaxis, where adrenaline is the treatment.
antihistamines.target: H1 histamine receptors on vessels, nerves and smooth muscle
classEffects: Drowsiness (marked with older agents), dry mouth, headache
cautions: Check driving response; avoid alcohol
Older agents cause confusion and falls in the elderly and urinary retention with prostate enlargement
Not a substitute for adrenaline in anaphylaxis

classWarnings.text: Sedating (first-generation) antihistamines cause drowsiness, impair driving and interact with alcohol and other sedatives; non-sedating antihistamines are preferred for daytime use and for older people.

classInteractions.with: Alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines and other sedatives (sedating antihistamines)
classInteractions.effect: Additive drowsiness and impaired coordination.
Additive dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and confusion in older people.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

ssris.name: SSRIs
ssris.summary: The most widely used antidepressants (sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), also first-line for anxiety disorders, panic, OCD and PTSD.
ssris.mechanism: SSRIs block the transporter that pumps serotonin back into nerve endings after release, so more remains in the synapse. The clinical benefit arrives over weeks as receptors adapt and neuroplasticity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex increases; the immediate rise in serotonin mostly produces the early side effects. They are generally safe in overdose and after heart attacks (sertraline).
classEffects: Nausea, headache, sleep change, sweating in the first weeks
Sexual dysfunction
Bleeding risk with NSAIDs and anticoagulants; low sodium in the elderly
cautions: Increased suicidal thoughts in the first weeks under 25: close follow-up
Taper rather than stop abruptly
Serotonin syndrome with tramadol, triptans, MAOIs and St John's wort
Citalopram prolongs the QT interval

classWarnings.text: Suicidal thoughts can increase in the first weeks, particularly under 25; close review is advised. Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, bleeding with NSAIDs and anticoagulants, hyponatraemia in older people and withdrawal symptoms on abrupt stopping are class effects.
Citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT interval in a dose-dependent way and have maximum doses, particularly over 65 and with other QT-prolonging drugs.

classInteractions.with: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, lithium, St John's wort
classInteractions.effect: Serotonin syndrome; MAOI combinations are contraindicated with washout periods.
Increased bleeding, particularly gastrointestinal; gastroprotection considered.
Additive QT prolongation.

duplicationRule.text: Two SSRIs together, or an SSRI with another serotonergic antidepressant, raise the risk of serotonin syndrome; switching is done with a planned cross-taper.

xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.name: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.summary: Medicines that lower uric acid by blocking the enzyme that makes it, dissolving the crystals that cause gout attacks and tophi when taken every day.
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid at the end of purine breakdown. Blocking it drops blood urate below its saturation point, so no new crystals form and existing deposits slowly dissolve. Attacks can increase for the first months as crystals mobilise, so an NSAID or colchicine is given as cover, and the dose is raised until the urate target is reached.
classEffects: Rash, nausea
Gout flares in the first months
cautions: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, rare but severe; HLA-B*58:01 screening in higher-risk populations
Interaction with azathioprine and mercaptopurine
Febuxostat: cardiovascular caution

classWarnings.text: Allopurinol can cause severe hypersensitivity (rash, fever, organ involvement), more often with kidney impairment, high starting doses and the HLA-B*58:01 allele common in some East Asian populations; any rash is a reason to stop. Starting treatment can provoke gout flares, so cover with an anti-inflammatory is given.

classInteractions.effect: Xanthine oxidase inhibition greatly increases their levels and toxicity (bone-marrow suppression); doses are cut to a quarter or the combination avoided.
Increased incidence of rash.
Increased risk of hypersensitivity reactions, particularly with kidney impairment.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

bisphosphonates.name: Bisphosphonates
bisphosphonates.summary: Medicines that slow bone loss by disabling the cells that dissolve bone, cutting hip and spine fractures in osteoporosis and treating Paget's disease and cancer in bone.
bisphosphonates.mechanism: Bisphosphonates bind bone mineral; when osteoclasts resorb that surface they absorb the drug, which disables their metabolism and triggers their death. Resorption falls while bone-building continues for a time, so density rises a few per cent and the bone's fine architecture is preserved. Weekly alendronate and risedronate, monthly ibandronate and yearly zoledronic acid infusions are the main forms.
classEffects: Indigestion and oesophageal irritation with tablets
Flu-like illness after the first infusion
Rarely osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures
cautions: Tablets taken upright with a full glass of water, 30 minutes before food
Correct vitamin D and calcium first; dental check
Not with eGFR below 35
Review after 3-5 years

classWarnings.text: Oral bisphosphonates can cause oesophageal irritation and ulceration; they are taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, standing or sitting upright for 30 minutes. Osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures are rare with long-term use; dental review is advised before starting.
Contraindicated in abnormalities of the oesophagus that delay emptying, in inability to stand or sit upright for 30 minutes, and in hypocalcaemia; vitamin D and calcium are corrected first.

classInteractions.with: Calcium, iron, antacids, food and drink other than water
classInteractions.effect: Markedly reduce absorption; taken at least 30 minutes before anything else.
Additive gastrointestinal irritation.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

macrolides.name: Macrolides
macrolides.summary: Antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins by binding the bacterial ribosome, used for chest, ear, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as the main alternative in penicillin allergy. Azithromycin, clarithromycin and erythromycin differ mainly in how long they last and how much they interact with other medicines.
macrolides.mechanism: Macrolides bind the 23S ribosomal RNA in the exit tunnel of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and block the growing peptide chain, halting protein synthesis; the effect is bacteriostatic against most organisms. They concentrate inside cells, including the white cells that travel to infected tissue, so they work against intracellular pathogens such as Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach. Erythromycin and clarithromycin are strong inhibitors of the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and of P-glycoprotein and so raise the levels of statins, calcium channel blockers, warfarin, some anticoagulants and many other drugs; azithromycin barely inhibits CYP3A4 and interacts less. All macrolides can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose azithromycin has anti-inflammatory effects used in COPD and bronchiectasis.
macrolides.target: 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain (most with erythromycin, which stimulates gut motility)
QT prolongation and arrhythmia, particularly with other QT-prolonging drugs or low potassium
Liver enzyme rise and cholestatic jaundice
Taste disturbance (clarithromycin), hearing loss with high or prolonged doses
cautions: Heart rhythm disorders, long QT, electrolyte disturbance
Liver disease
Myasthenia gravis
Clarithromycin and erythromycin: many interactions through CYP3A4 (statins, some anticoagulants, calcium channel blockers, colchicine, warfarin)

classWarnings.text: All macrolides can prolong the QT interval and have been associated with torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death; risk is greatest with other QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and existing heart disease.

Clarithromycin and erythromycin are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors: simvastatin and some other statins, colchicine, ticagrelor and several other drugs are contraindicated or need dose reduction while they are taken. Azithromycin lacks most of these interactions.

classInteractions.with: Statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin) with clarithromycin or erythromycin
classInteractions.effect: Greatly increased statin levels and rhabdomyolysis risk; simvastatin is contraindicated with clarithromycin and paused during erythromycin.
Raised INR with any macrolide; extra INR checks.

classInteractions.with: Other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, sotalol, some antipsychotics and antidepressants, quinolones)
classInteractions.effect: Additive QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk.

classInteractions.with: Colchicine, digoxin, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, some DOACs (with clarithromycin or erythromycin)
classInteractions.effect: Raised levels through CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition; colchicine with clarithromycin is contraindicated in kidney or liver impairment.

duplicationRule.text: Two macrolides together add QT prolongation and gut side effects without benefit.

vaccines-influenza.name: Influenza vaccines
vaccines-influenza.summary: Seasonal vaccines against influenza A and B, reformulated every year: inactivated injected vaccines for most people and a live attenuated nasal spray for children.
vaccines-influenza.mechanism: Each formulation presents the immune system with haemagglutinin from the strains expected that season, either as inactivated virus fragments or, in the nasal spray, as weakened live viruses that replicate only in the cooler nose. Antibodies and memory cells form over about two weeks; the antibodies neutralise the virus at the airway surface and the memory cells speed the response if infection occurs. Because circulating strains drift, the strains are reselected annually and immunity from one season fades.
classEffects: Sore arm, mild fever and aches for a day or two
Nasal congestion after the live nasal spray
cautions: Previous severe allergic reaction to the vaccine
The live nasal spray is avoided in significant immunosuppression, pregnancy and severe asthma
Postponed during a feverish illness

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

contrast-agents.name: Contrast agents
contrast-agents.summary: Substances given to make blood vessels, organs, the gut or joints stand out on imaging: iodinated agents for X-ray and CT, gadolinium agents for MRI, microbubbles for ultrasound and barium for the gut.
contrast-agents.mechanism: Each agent changes how the tissue it fills interacts with the imaging energy. Iodine and barium absorb X-rays, so filled vessels and cavities appear bright on X-ray and CT; gadolinium shortens the relaxation time of nearby water protons, brightening perfused tissue on MRI; microbubbles reflect ultrasound strongly and outline blood flow. Timing the scan to when the agent is in arteries, veins or tissue shows different structures.
contrast-agents.target: The imaging signal of the tissue the agent occupies (X-ray attenuation, MRI relaxation, ultrasound reflection)
classEffects: A warm flush, metallic taste and nausea during injection
Allergic-type reactions, rarely severe
Kidney injury with iodinated agents in people at risk; gadolinium retention concerns in repeated MRI
cautions: Kidney function checked before iodinated and gadolinium agents in people at risk
Previous contrast reactions and severe allergy declared beforehand
Pregnancy: used only when the imaging is essential

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.name: Diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.summary: Radioactive medicines given in tiny amounts so that a gamma camera or PET scanner can show where they accumulate: bone turnover, blood flow to the heart, thyroid activity, glucose use by tumours.
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.mechanism: A radioactive isotope is attached to a molecule the body handles in a known way: a phosphate analogue that binds forming bone, a glucose analogue trapped in metabolically active cells, iodine taken up by the thyroid, or a compound retained by well-perfused heart muscle. The radiation the isotope emits is detected from outside and mapped, so the image shows function rather than anatomy; combining it with CT adds the anatomy. The radiation dose is kept low by using short-lived isotopes and small amounts.
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.target: Physiological processes (bone turnover, perfusion, glucose metabolism, receptor binding) imaged through the tracer's distribution
classEffects: A small radiation dose; reactions to the tracer itself are rare
cautions: Pregnancy and breastfeeding declared before the injection
Radiation-safety advice for the hours after the scan (fluids, bladder emptying, distance from pregnant women and young children)
Preparation specific to the tracer: fasting for FDG, medicine timing for perfusion studies
